medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reviews a fictional biopsy-proven localized colon adenocarcinoma. What is the most defensible broad next-step framing for an educational MDT discussion?

options.text: Treat every colon lesion identically without regard to stage or patient context.
Integrate stage, pathology, imaging, patient factors and multidisciplinary options; colon resection is a principal treatment in appropriate localized disease.
Infer a definitive operation from one CT image alone.
Assume a public course certifies operative readiness.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI's professional PDQ describes stage-dependent management and surgery as primary treatment in appropriate localized colon cancer; planning depends on stage and context, not a single image or course certificate.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional rectal cancer case includes MRI information and a question of sphincter preservation. Which discussion best reflects the evidence framework?

options.text: Use rectal MRI, pathology and multidisciplinary review; weigh oncologic margins, treatment response, function and patient goals.
Apply the colon cancer pathway without modification.
Assume sphincter preservation is always preferable regardless of margins or expected function.
Choose surgery based only on age.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI notes rectal cancer management differs because local recurrence risk, radiation and surgical technique matter; a multidisciplinary team is central. The 2025 open review likewise describes MRI-guided planning and functional trade-offs.

practiceQuestions.stem: The ABCRS public description says what about its written Part I?

options.text: A single general surgery examination replaces it.
A six-hour multiple-choice exam spanning colon and rectal surgery, including radiology, pathology and pertinent basic science.
It is a technical skills test performed during this online course.
It has a guaranteed pass threshold after 36 lecture hours.

practiceQuestions.rationale: This restates the Board's own public description. There is no course-derived pass guarantee, and exam eligibility remains controlled by ABCRS.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about ABCRS oral Part II eligibility is supported by the Board's current public page?

options.text: A learner may take Part II after watching this curriculum.
ABS certification and passing the ABCRS written examination are required before oral Part II.
Only an ABS written exam is needed; there is no colorectal exam.
Eligibility is granted by an independent course provider.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABCRS states that oral candidates must have passed the ABCRS written exam and be certified by ABS, in addition to professional requirements. Only the Board decides individual eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional colorectal surgery patient deteriorates and one inflammatory marker is elevated. Which reasoning is safest for an educational case discussion?

options.text: The marker alone proves an anastomotic leak.
Ignore the change because markers are never useful.
Treat the trend as one input, reassess the whole trajectory and differential, and escalate evaluation to the responsible clinical team.
Delay review until a course quiz is completed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A single finding is not a diagnosis. The original pilot and source material emphasize contextual interpretation, differentials and clinical escalation rather than an unsupported threshold or remote treatment instruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the correct way to use an older lecture on enhanced recovery when current policy is needed?

options.text: Follow it as the current universal standard because it is a video.
Treat it as historical teaching and verify details against the current ASCRS/SAGES guideline and local policy.
Discard all guidelines and rely on the speaker's preferences.
Assume watching it confers clinical authorization.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The UC Davis lecture was presented in 2016; the ASCRS/SAGES guideline is newer (2022), and local protocols and later updates should be checked. Neither video substitutes for credentialing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A published Radiopaedia colon CT case is used for classroom discussion. What is the appropriate rights-conscious practice?

options.text: Download and embed images because free viewing equals permission to rehost.
Link to the source; if any reuse is contemplated, follow its CC BY-NC-SA attribution/share-alike/noncommercial terms and verify suitability.
Remove author and case ID attribution.
Present it as a synthetic image.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia describes its cases as CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 and requires attribution; this course links only and does not copy or rehost. The case's de-identification provenance is not independently audited.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description best distinguishes the supplied BIDMC fellowship page from the Johns Hopkins colorectal page reviewed?

options.text: Both pages were confirmed to describe the same combined fellowship.
BIDMC describes a 12-month ACGME-accredited clinical fellowship; the Hopkins page reviewed describes a clinical care division, not a distinct fellowship offering.
The BIDMC page describes research-only postdoctoral training.
Neither is an official institutional page.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The institutional pages were read directly. The course preserves the exact BIDMC offering and does not infer a Hopkins programme variant from a clinical service page.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about a published CT finding in the linked colon cancer case is methodologically sound?

options.text: A radiologic appearance alone equals histopathology and complete stage.
Distinguish imaging finding from the case's reported pathology result and seek full clinical staging context.
A single case estimates population risk.
The image is synthetic and may be freely altered.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The case page describes increased wall thickness and pericolic findings and separately reports pathology-proven adenocarcinoma. A single case cannot establish a population estimate or provide complete staging.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fellow-in-training asks whether completion of this independent course can count as BIDMC clinical case volume or ABCRS eligibility. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Yes, if 36 hours are watched.
No; only accredited supervised training, board rules, case documentation and Board review determine those requirements.
Yes, if the learner passes original practice questions.
Yes, if the videos show operative cases.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The curriculum has no clinical patients, operative supervision, case logs, skills assessment, accreditation or authority to confer eligibility; ABCRS rules specify actual accredited training and Board review.

topicGaps: No new external recording was added: the directly relevant ACS videos reviewed did not expose a reliable observed-runtime field in the accessible source, and one ACS-linked course directs learners to LMS/store access. Their timestamps/title or advertised CME length are not substituted for recording runtime.

All ten ABS QE content categories (breast, colorectal, cutaneous, endocrine, HPB, sarcoma, peritoneal malignancy, thoracic, upper GI, and miscellaneous medical knowledge) still lack verified, free, observed-runtime core lecture hours in this evidence set; the existing NIH recording remains a non-core supplement.

Source-backed full original scripts were authored for cross-site diagnostic/staging reasoning, sarcoma biopsy planning, pancreatic imaging/CA 19-9 interpretation, and peritoneal malignancy evidence/symptom-intent discussions. They are scripted only—not recordings, rendered hours, or competency evidence.

Topic-specific video gaps remain for detailed breast, colorectal subsites/appendix/rectum/anus, cutaneous, endocrine, liver/biliary, pancreatic endocrine, GIST/desmoid, mesothelioma, thoracic, upper-GI/small bowel, pathology/radiation/systemic therapy complications, follow-up, trial interpretation, palliation, quality, rehabilitation, and equity.

A 36-hour, 36-lesson source-mapped production plan is proposed, but its target minutes are planning estimates only and are excluded from all observed-hour totals; lesson-level factual scripts and recording verification remain future work.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet-listed Johns Hopkins offering only; the Hopkins official directory classifies the programme as ACGME Accredited and lists a 2-year duration. The department describes two named match tracks, shared initial clinical rotations (GI/HPB, colorectal, breast, melanoma/sarcoma, endocrine, medical oncology and radiation oncology) and weekly conferences. The General/Research track is still clinical fellowship education; the research component is not a separate physician specialty. The HPB track remains within CGSO. No Harvard affiliate offering was in this item packet; no Harvard variant is inferred. SSO says all US programmes on its CGSO list are ACGME-accredited. Public pages do not expose the full internal didactic set or actual Hopkins rotation quantities.
sourceCaveats: Current point-in-time check. Johns Hopkins fellowship directory lists ACGME-accredited and two-year; program description provides tracks and rotations but not a complete public syllabus or didactic-hour ledger.
ABS CGSO blueprint is the publicly posted 2022 revision, updated January 2023; it is an approximate exam blueprint, not a syllabus, certification guarantee, or promise of exam contents.
ACGME PDF is the July 2026-effective requirements (with an announced interim update); requirements govern accredited graduate training, not this self-study.

NCI PDQ summaries consulted here display latest updates in 2025. The pancreatic, gastric, soft-tissue sarcoma and other summaries cite earlier AJCC editions in sections; confirm current staging standards and current specialty guidelines before clinical use.
Current CAP page reports September 2026 updates; linked CAP PDF is copyrighted and its use is restricted by CAP terms.
TCIA public access is subject to agreement and dataset-specific terms. Authentic/de-identified does not mean permitted to copy, redistribute or use as a complete diagnostic case.

NIH lecture duration is observed on its public runtime field, but subject matter is supplemental and not credited to the CGSO core minimum. YouTube candidates were not included because runtime/free accessibility could not be independently observed through the stateless metadata attempt.
The SSO CGSO board-review course is described as a distinct virtual course; no login-only/proprietary course hours are claimed or counted.
No patient records or clinical images were copied into these files. Case vignettes are explicitly fictional.

topicGaps: No new external recording was added: the directly relevant ACS videos reviewed did not expose a reliable observed-runtime field in the accessible source, and one ACS-linked course directs learners to LMS/store access. Their timestamps/title or advertised CME length are not substituted for recording runtime.

All ten ABS QE content categories (breast, colorectal, cutaneous, endocrine, HPB, sarcoma, peritoneal malignancy, thoracic, upper GI, and miscellaneous medical knowledge) still lack verified, free, observed-runtime core lecture hours in this evidence set; the existing NIH recording remains a non-core supplement.

Source-backed full original scripts were authored for cross-site diagnostic/staging reasoning, sarcoma biopsy planning, pancreatic imaging/CA 19-9 interpretation, and peritoneal malignancy evidence/symptom-intent discussions. They are scripted only—not recordings, rendered hours, or competency evidence.

Topic-specific video gaps remain for detailed breast, colorectal subsites/appendix/rectum/anus, cutaneous, endocrine, liver/biliary, pancreatic endocrine, GIST/desmoid, mesothelioma, thoracic, upper-GI/small bowel, pathology/radiation/systemic therapy complications, follow-up, trial interpretation, palliation, quality, rehabilitation, and equity.

A 36-hour, 36-lesson source-mapped production plan is proposed, but its target minutes are planning estimates only and are excluded from all observed-hour totals; lesson-level factual scripts and recording verification remain future work.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a suspicious breast lesion and imaging raises a second ipsilateral focus. Which principle best fits the NCI health-professional summary before an irreversible treatment plan is chosen?

options.text: Treat the MRI appearance as diagnostic and proceed without tissue confirmation.
Confirm diagnosis and stage; obtain pathologic confirmation of an MRI-positive finding before treatment decisions based on it.
Use a serum marker instead of biopsy.
Assume multifocality means metastatic disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI PDQ frames management as confirmation of diagnosis, stage evaluation and therapy selection; it notes that only a minority of MRI-positive findings represent malignancy and recommends pathologic confirmation before treatment. This is a study principle, not patient advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which biomarker set is identified by the NCI breast PDQ as important in determining prognosis and predicting response to endocrine or HER2-directed therapy?

options.text: ER, PR and HER2 status
CEA, CA 19-9 and AFP
Breslow thickness, ulceration and mitotic rate
Only tumor size on imaging

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI summary identifies ER/PR and HER2 as relevant prognostic/predictive markers; the overall plan remains integrated with stage, grade, histology and patient context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A question asks whether serum CEA is appropriate as a population screening test for colorectal cancer. Which statement is supported by the NCI colon PDQ?

options.text: CEA is a valuable stand-alone screening test.
CEA is not valuable as a screening test because false-positive and false-negative results limit it.
CEA is diagnostic of metastatic disease when elevated.
CEA should replace colon evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI PDQ says CEA is not valuable for screening due to false positives and false negatives; its postoperative use is restricted to patients who would be candidates for metastasectomy, and CEA alone is not a routine response-monitoring strategy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A suspicious pigmented lesion is being evaluated in a fictional patient. Which diagnostic approach does the NCI melanoma PDQ prefer?

options.text: Shave the lesion and cauterize the base.
Perform a biopsy, preferably local excision, and avoid shave/cautery that could compromise microstaging.
Begin systemic treatment based on ABCDE features alone.
Defer tissue diagnosis until imaging proves metastasis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI PDQ says suspicious lesions should be biopsied, preferably by local excision, and should not be shaved or cauterized; a pathologist can then assess microstaging.

practiceQuestions.stem: Before intervention for a suspected soft-tissue sarcoma, what process best reduces the risk that the diagnostic procedure compromises later curative resection?

options.text: Unplanned excision by whichever service is available.
Coordinate biopsy planning among the sarcoma surgeon, radiologist and pathologist, with image-guided core biopsy or planned incisional biopsy as appropriate.
Begin radiation before obtaining adequate tissue.
Rely on imaging alone to define histology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI sarcoma PDQ stresses adequate core or planned incisional biopsy, expert pathology review and planning with the surgeon, radiation oncologist and interventional radiologist so the initial biopsy does not compromise later resection.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which interpretation of CA 19-9 is consistent with the NCI pancreatic cancer PDQ?

options.text: A normal result excludes pancreatic cancer recurrence.
It is tumor-specific and determines resectability by itself.
It has low specificity; a normal value does not preclude recurrence, so it cannot replace imaging and multidisciplinary assessment.
It replaces tissue diagnosis and staging imaging.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI PDQ states no tumor-specific pancreatic marker exists, CA 19-9 has low specificity and a normal result does not preclude recurrence. Resectability evaluation requires a broader clinical and imaging assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: According to the ABS CGSO QE blueprint page reviewed for this course, what approximate proportion of the examination belongs to Section 1 Patient Care, with the remainder designated Miscellaneous Medical Knowledge?
practiceQuestions.rationale: The public ABS blueprint assigns approximately 88% to site-specific Patient Care and 12% to Miscellaneous Medical Knowledge; actual examination percentages may vary slightly year to year.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly describes ABS initial certification in CGSO?

options.text: A public video course alone confers CGSO board certification.
Candidates need neither general surgery certification nor a separate exam.

ABS CGSO certification requires the prescribed training/eligibility requirements and passing both a CGSO Qualifying Examination and a Certifying Examination; primary surgery certification is required.
The HPB institutional track awards an unrelated board certificate automatically.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABS identifies two CGSO exams, QE and CE, and requires primary certification in surgery as part of the process. The Johns Hopkins institutional track names do not constitute separate board credentials.

practiceQuestions.stem: A primary peritoneal/ovarian-type fictional tumor is discussed at conference. Which statement is supported by the NCI ovarian/fallopian/primary-peritoneal PDQ?

options.text: Primary peritoneal and fallopian tube carcinomas must always use entirely unrelated management frameworks.

These epithelial Müllerian-site cancers are commonly grouped together in staging/treatment because of shared origin hypotheses and similar management, while case-specific assessment remains necessary.
CA-125 is sufficiently specific for population screening of asymptomatic people.
Surgery is appropriate regardless of disease extent or patient condition.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI PDQ explains that ovarian epithelial, fallopian tube and primary peritoneal cancers are often considered together because of shared Müllerian biology and similar management. It also describes limited screening test predictive value and individualized treatment assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional retrospective follow-up study reports more recurrence detection after frequent imaging, but no randomized comparison and no demonstrated overall-survival benefit. What is the best evidence-focused response?

options.text: Conclude that the imaging schedule improves survival.
Separate earlier detection from improved patient outcomes, examine selection/bias and uncertainty, and do not infer a survival benefit not shown.
Ignore study design because the endpoint is intuitive.
Apply the result to every tumor site without checking applicability.

practiceQuestions.rationale: This is an original research-interpretation question aligned to the ABS blueprint’s trials/ethics/bias domain. NCI colon PDQ notes limited high-level evidence for follow-up and that standard postoperative monitoring has not shown an overall-survival benefit in large randomized trials.

title: Complex Spine Reconstruction Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent self-study analogue; not fellowship training)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Advanced physician-level self-study audience: completion of medical school and core orthopaedic surgery or neurological surgery residency-level knowledge assumed; not an entry pathway for unlicensed learners.
Competency in spinal anatomy, neurological localization, imaging fundamentals, evidence appraisal, perioperative medicine and basic spine pathology.
This curriculum cannot substitute for supervised clinical training, hands-on lab, clinical privileging, institutional credentialing or individualized patient care.
Learners should check current board rules directly with ABOS/ABNS; the fellowship course itself does not provide certification eligibility.
objectives: Construct a structured differential from history, neurological examination and cervical/thoracolumbar imaging while distinguishing radiographic abnormalities from clinical syndromes.
Summarize evidence and uncertainty for common degenerative disease, trauma, deformity, neoplasm and infection presentations without converting educational rules into universal treatment indications.
Interpret standing and dynamic alignment images in the context of symptoms, flexibility, compensatory mechanisms, bone health and patient goals.
Compare treatment options and risks using shared decision-making, comorbidity/frailty assessment, multidisciplinary optimization and explicit alternatives.
Recognize time-sensitive neurological deterioration, suspected cord compression, infection and trauma that require urgent real-world evaluation.
Appraise complication mechanisms, revision scenarios, outcome measures, ethics, consent and quality improvement.
Explain the difference between institutional program design, ACGME standards, core-specialty board certification and a nonexistent separate spine-board examination.

units.title: Clinical framework, anatomy and localization
objectives: Localize cord, root and cauda equina findings; develop a focused differential.
topics: Cervical, thoracic, lumbar and lumbopelvic anatomy; neurological examination; red flags; patient goals and functional history.
boardDomains: Core orthopaedic/neurosurgical knowledge; diagnosis and data interpretation (curricular mapping only, not a published spine exam blueprint).
units.casePractice: Use a fictional vignette to separate myelopathy, radiculopathy, axial pain and non-spinal mimics; do not diagnose from imaging alone.
units.assessment: One-page localization map; rubric: neuroanatomy 40%, differential and red flags 30%, communication/uncertainty 30%.

units.title: Spine imaging and diagnostic reasoning
objectives: Select imaging questions and interpret the limits of radiographs, CT and MRI.
topics: Standing full-length alignment, MRI cord/root and soft tissue, CT bone/instrumentation, dynamic views when clinically appropriate, artifact and imaging-symptom concordance.
boardDomains: Diagnostic imaging and interpretation; evidence-based decision-making.
units.casePractice: Linked authentic published cases only; learner records the question each modality can answer and a competing explanation.
units.assessment: Structured image-report exercise with no copied images; rubric: sequence/quality 25%, findings 35%, clinical correlation and limitations 40%.

units.title: Degenerative cervical disease and myelopathy
objectives: Classify symptomatic DCM severity, summarize guideline choices and flag neurological decline.
topics: DCM, radiculopathy, cord compression, mJOA limitations, anterior/posterior approach equipoise in selected anatomy, follow-up and shared decision-making.
boardDomains: Degenerative disease; diagnosis; management; complication counseling.
units.casePractice: Compare fictional mild, moderate and severe DCM vignettes with and without radiculopathy; do not infer a universal operation.
units.assessment: Guideline recommendation matrix with population, recommendation strength, evidence and caveat columns; rubric: accurate strata 40%, evidence strength 30%, safety/communication 30%.

units.title: Degenerative lumbar disease and stenosis
objectives: Distinguish stenosis, instability, deformity and nonspecific pain; critically assess indication claims.
topics: Clinical-imaging concordance, non-operative options, decompression/fusion decision concepts, adjacent disease and outcome measures.
boardDomains: Degenerative spine; treatment planning; outcomes and risks.
units.casePractice: Use open guideline links and synthetic text-only vignettes; document evidence gaps and competing diagnoses.
units.assessment: Evidence table for a clinical question; rubric: PICO clarity 25%, source quality 35%, balanced interpretation 40%.

units.title: Adult spinal deformity phenotype and goals
objectives: Describe deformity by coronal/sagittal alignment, symptoms, flexibility, compensation, and functional aims.
topics: Degenerative and iatrogenic deformity, sagittal modifiers, pelvic parameters, global balance, age/health context and patient-reported outcomes.
boardDomains: Deformity; imaging; clinical reasoning and goals of care.
units.casePractice: Analyze AO Spine/peer-reviewed case material through publisher links; no images are downloaded or rehosted.
units.assessment: Write an alignment phenotype plus three competing explanations; rubric: measurements 25%, compensation 25%, goals/uncertainty 50%.

units.title: Reconstruction planning and osteotomy concepts
objectives: Explain principles, tradeoffs and risk discussions for staged/limited versus extensive reconstruction without creating an operative recipe.
topics: Correction targets as individualized estimates; flexibility; interbody strategies; osteotomy risk categories; neurologic/vascular risk and contingency planning.
boardDomains: Surgical judgment; technical knowledge; informed consent.
units.casePractice: Conference-style fictional plan comparison with explicit assumptions, risk/benefit and reasons to defer.
units.assessment: Multidisciplinary preoperative conference memo; rubric: evidence/alternatives 30%, risk mitigation 30%, clarity 20%, limits and consent 20%.

units.title: Bone health, frailty and perioperative optimization
objectives: Identify modifiable risks and explain why optimization is individualized.
topics: Bone health assessment, nutrition, smoking, frailty, cardiopulmonary risk, thrombosis, mental health, rehabilitation and multidisciplinary planning.
units.casePractice: Create a fictional risk/optimization checklist; avoid prescriptions or fixed treatment thresholds unsupported by source.
units.assessment: Checklist and shared-decision note; rubric: comprehensive risks 35%, actionable team coordination 35%, patient preferences 30%.

units.title: Spinal trauma and instability
objectives: Apply evidence-based diagnostic framing and recognize uncertain evidence in adult thoracolumbar injury.
topics: Neurological status, imaging, classification limits, stabilization concepts, timing, VTE prophylaxis and multidisciplinary trauma care.
units.casePractice: Use CNS guideline chapters and fictional cases; do not give individual trauma-management directions.
units.assessment: Claim-evidence audit of one recommendation; rubric: population fit 30%, evidence and date 35%, uncertainty 35%.

units.title: Spinal neoplasm and metastatic cord compression
objectives: Recognize urgent features and frame multidisciplinary oncologic spinal assessment.
topics: Neurologic compromise, mechanical stability, tumor biology, imaging, systemic disease, goals and coordination with oncology/radiation oncology.
boardDomains: Spinal oncology; urgent neurological diagnosis; shared care.
units.casePractice: Read public NICE guidance and linked educational case resources; do not copy patient images or extrapolate a single-treatment rule.
units.assessment: Urgent-referral pathway diagram and patient-centered alternatives; rubric: red-flag recognition 35%, team pathway 35%, limits 30%.

units.title: Spinal infection and postoperative infection
objectives: Develop a differential and identify need for urgent evaluation without prescribing a regimen.
topics: Discitis/osteomyelitis, epidural infection, host risk factors, imaging/labs/cultures, source control concepts and implant-associated infection.
units.casePractice: Fictional differential exercise; link to public cases only, with explicit not-medical-advice caveat.
units.assessment: Differential and escalation memo; rubric: emergency recognition 30%, tests/differential 35%, uncertainty 35%.

units.title: Complications, revision and quality
objectives: Classify mechanical, neurological, infectious and medical complications and propose learning-system responses.
topics: Junctional failure, pseudarthrosis, implant failure, neurologic injury, revision decision process, adverse-event communication, patient-reported outcomes and QI.
boardDomains: Complications; outcomes; professionalism and quality improvement.
units.casePractice: Analyze public educational scenarios and event-analysis methods; no actual medical records.
units.assessment: Non-punitive root-cause analysis on a fictional event; rubric: system factors 35%, patient communication 30%, measurable action 35%.

units.title: Ethics, evidence synthesis and board literacy
objectives: Separate program rules, board requirements, clinical evidence and educational claims; present a defensible case conference.
topics: Consent, conflicts, evidence certainty, limits of self-study, exact ABOS/ABNS pathways, ACGME versus Non-Standard institutional label, research literacy.
boardDomains: Professionalism; ethics; evidence-based practice; core specialty board awareness.
units.casePractice: Critique one primary source and one guideline plus a fictional multidisciplinary presentation.
units.assessment: Capstone 10-minute oral presentation plus written references; rubric: clinical reasoning 30%, evidence 25%, risk/ethics 25%, communication 20%.

assignment.title: Multidisciplinary reconstruction conference portfolio (fictional case only)
deliverables: A text-only patient profile with stated assumptions and goals; no real patient data or copied clinical images.
Differential and concise neurological/imaging problem representation; no unsupported definitive diagnosis.
Evidence table covering at least two management alternatives and their risks/uncertainties.
Preoperative optimization and contingency checklist, consent considerations and team roles.
Reflection on where additional real-world supervision, specialty input or current guidance is required.
assignment.passNote: Formative scoring only; not validated for board prediction or clinical competency.

assessment.format: 12 unit formative checks, 8 original educational questions, one portfolio and a capstone case conference.
assessment.rubric: Knowledge and evidence 40%; clinical reasoning and alternatives 30%; safety/uncertainty 20%; communication 10%.
assessment.limitations: No standardized or validated exam, no real patient management, no official ABOS/ABNS examination content, no prediction or guarantee of passing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, hyperreflexia and cervical cord compression with progressive clinical findings. Which statement best reflects the 2017 AO Spine/CSRS guideline?

options.text: Surgery is recommended for moderate and severe DCM; treatment for mild disease allows more than one evidence-supported option.
Prophylactic surgery is recommended for every person with cord compression on MRI.
MRI compression without examination findings establishes severe DCM.
The guideline requires the same approach for every patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline strongly recommends surgery for moderate/severe DCM; for mild DCM it suggests surgery or supervised structured rehabilitation, with surgery for deterioration or failure to improve. Imaging alone does not establish clinical severity; approach is individualized.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult has MRI evidence of cervical cord compression but no myelopathic signs/symptoms and no radiculopathy. Which option matches the 2017 guideline?

options.text: Offer prophylactic surgery to all such patients.
Do not routinely offer prophylactic surgery; counsel on progression symptoms and follow clinically.
No further clinical discussion is necessary.
Treat as severe DCM based on imaging.

practiceQuestions.rationale: For nonmyelopathic cord compression without radiculopathy, the guideline suggests no prophylactic surgery, education about progression symptoms and clinical follow-up. Radiculopathy changes the risk discussion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A team compares anterior and posterior surgery for a fictional DCM presentation in which either approach is anatomically reasonable. What does the 2025 AO Spine recommendation support?

options.text: Anterior surgery is always superior.
Posterior surgery is always safer.
There is equipoise in physical-function outcomes when either approach can be used, with different complication profiles to consider.
The evidence proves both techniques are identical in every outcome.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 review gives a strong recommendation that there is equipoise in outcomes for cases where either approach can be used, while complication profiles differ; this is not a universal equivalence claim.
practiceQuestions.domain: Evidence appraisal and DCM approach discussion

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is given a standing full-length image with sagittal imbalance but has no symptoms/examination or flexibility data. What is the soundest next reasoning step?

options.text: Prescribe a fixed correction target from the image alone.
Integrate symptoms, neurological examination, compensatory posture, flexibility, bone/medical context and patient goals before considering management options.
Assume the finding is a surgical indication.
Infer surgical competence from this measurement.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Adult deformity assessment is multidimensional. Classification/review literature and the public Hopkins curriculum emphasize clinical evaluation, goals, imaging and mentored planning; a single alignment image cannot establish an individual indication or target.

practiceQuestions.stem: A question asks whether a Hopkins fellowship is ACGME-accredited because ACGME has a 12-month Orthopaedic Surgery of the Spine program requirement. Which answer is correct from the reviewed sources?

options.text: Yes; the general ACGME program requirement proves accreditation of every named fellowship.
No conclusion about Hopkins accreditation follows: the Hopkins directory labels this offering Non-Standard; the ACGME document describes a separate program category.
It is a residency because it is 12 months.
The fellowship creates a spine-board certificate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A general specialty requirement and institution-specific accreditation status are distinct. Hopkins' official directory explicitly labels this fellowship Non-Standard; no separate board credential follows from that label.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with known malignancy develops new progressive limb weakness and possible spinal cord compression. Which learning response is safest?

options.text: Reassure and schedule routine review because spinal metastases are rarely urgent.
Recognize possible metastatic spinal cord compression and follow urgent local escalation/referral pathways; do not use this self-study course as individual treatment advice.
Choose a definitive operation from a lecture video.
Wait until an elective follow-up regardless of progression.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE NG234 covers recognition, referral, investigation and management of spinal metastases/MSCC. New neurological deterioration is time-sensitive and requires real-world urgent clinical assessment and local protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: When applying CNS thoracolumbar trauma guidelines, what limitation should an evidence appraiser note?

options.text: Their underlying systematic search extended through March 31, 2015, and the guideline authors describe areas of limited/heterogeneous evidence; current protocols and newer updates must be checked.
They constitute an individual patient's operative order.
They prove every treatment question has high-certainty evidence.
They are a board examination blueprint.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The CNS methodology page gives the search date and notes heterogeneity and gaps in evidence. Guidelines are educational aids for qualified clinicians, not patient-specific orders or board blueprints.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner finishes this online curriculum after reading that the institutional fellowship accepts orthopaedic and neurological surgery residency graduates. What credential/eligibility follows from the online course?

options.text: ABOS and ABNS eligibility automatically.
A separate spine board certificate.
No board eligibility, licensure, clinical training credit or procedure competence; board rules are independently determined by ABOS/ABNS.
Automatic admission to the Hopkins fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The course is independent self-study. ABOS and ABNS certify core specialties with separate board-defined requirements; neither Hopkins institutional training nor this curriculum is granted by completion here.

topicGaps: Verified recordings remain a partial lecture supplement rather than a complete general-surgery curriculum. No qualifying recordings in this ledger provide substantial teaching across U01 preoperative evaluation/perioperative care, U02 abdominal wall/hernia, U04 esophagus/stomach/upper-GI bleeding, or broad U05 small-bowel, appendiceal, diverticular, rectal and anorectal disease.

Organ-specific gaps remain substantial: U03 has one pancreatic-cancer grand-rounds recording but no verified comprehensive biliary/liver/pancreas/spleen curriculum; U06 has stage-0 breast and adrenal incidentaloma talks but not broad breast, thyroid/parathyroid, melanoma or soft-tissue teaching; U09 has a venous-disease recording but no verified arterial, vascular-access, thoracic, pediatric or transplant teaching.

U07/U08/U10 have multiple short foundational recordings and added grand rounds, but this does not establish comprehensive surgical critical-care, infection/source-control, trauma/burn, endoscopy, MIS, or technical competence. Grand rounds are topic-specific, not systematic lessons across the domain.

Surgical oncology/U11 coverage remains incomplete: breast stage-0 and pancreatic-cancer recordings are narrow talks and do not substitute for staging, multidisciplinary decision-making, tumor biology, evidence appraisal, or outcomes instruction across general surgery.

Verified observed free recordings total 22.1875 hours, of which 8.4136 are categorized specialty and 13.7739 foundation. The 13.8125-hour floor gap remains real; original authored scripts and planned clips are not rendered or counted.

For the 50 pre-existing YouTube items, the original ledger reports durations from public playlist metadata but individual playback was not independently verified because of HTTP 429/403 throttling. The seven added Utah Kaltura pages returned HTTP 200 and exposed durations, player and download links; playback and clinical content were not independently quality-reviewed.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: General Surgery is a board-certification specialty with a two-exam ABS pathway: QE followed by CE. The GSQE content outline and SCORE 2025–2026 curriculum outline inform this course. QE outline page updated 2021; exam rules are date-sensitive and must be checked on ABS pages.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent education does not confer board eligibility. ABS eligibility requires qualifying accredited graduate medical training and satisfaction of current training, operative log, documentation, licensure and other board rules. The GSCE requires the QE and a full unrestricted U.S. or Canadian medical license for registration; confirm exact current requirements directly with ABS. A learner’s completion, score, or certificate here provides no ABS status.

officialProgrammes.name: General Surgery Training Program (categorical and preliminary resident tracks; official page heading)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes five clinical PGY years for categorical residents and a preliminary track for broad training without expectation of completing at Johns Hopkins. ACGME requires a 60-month educational program; the Hopkins page also describes a one- to four-year research experience but does not clearly reconcile the research interval with calendar duration. It lists selected PGY 1–5 rotations and weekly didactics/simulation-center teaching; it is not a complete lecture syllabus or public case volume database. The page states post-chief-year eligibility to take ABS examinations, contingent on all current ABS requirements. It names advanced fellowships but they are not included as separate tracks here.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Only one distinct physician training specialty was established from packet: Johns Hopkins General Surgery Training Program. Its official page identifies categorical and preliminary residency tracks, and separately describes advanced fellowships as subsequent options; those fellowships are not merged into this course. Preliminary residents are not treated as the five-year categorical track. The course is not the institution’s course. Harvard affiliation was not identified as a variant for this assigned item.
sourceCaveats: Johns Hopkins program page gives selected rotations, not a full syllabus. It describes five clinical PGY years and a one- to four-year research experience; the relationship of those descriptions to total calendar duration is not fully clear from the public page. The 60-month ACGME requirement is a separate program standard, not a claim about the precise Hopkins calendar path. Verify details with the program.
ACGME program requirements set minimum program standards and a 60-month length; they are not an ABS content blueprint or Johns Hopkins schedule.
ABS QE content outline last marked updated 2021; SCORE outline is 2025–2026. Board exam rules/eligibility should be rechecked on ABS at time of application.
ACS Case Reviews says the archive was open access but the journal has been discontinued; case listing failed to load during check and the page says it will disappear Jan. 1, 2027.
Human clinical review was not performed. All clinical content is educational and must be checked against current sources, applicable jurisdiction, institutional policy and qualified clinicians.

YouTube duration evidence is metadata-derived from public listings, and direct playback was not individually verified due throttling. Public access does not imply redistribution license. No content copied or rehosted.
No public open institutional Johns Hopkins lecture library totaling 36 specialty-specific hours was verified in this pass; all generated production plans remain planned, not ready videos.
No patient records, images, protected cases, actual board questions, or private data included.

topicGaps: Verified recordings remain a partial lecture supplement rather than a complete general-surgery curriculum. No qualifying recordings in this ledger provide substantial teaching across U01 preoperative evaluation/perioperative care, U02 abdominal wall/hernia, U04 esophagus/stomach/upper-GI bleeding, or broad U05 small-bowel, appendiceal, diverticular, rectal and anorectal disease.

Organ-specific gaps remain substantial: U03 has one pancreatic-cancer grand-rounds recording but no verified comprehensive biliary/liver/pancreas/spleen curriculum; U06 has stage-0 breast and adrenal incidentaloma talks but not broad breast, thyroid/parathyroid, melanoma or soft-tissue teaching; U09 has a venous-disease recording but no verified arterial, vascular-access, thoracic, pediatric or transplant teaching.

U07/U08/U10 have multiple short foundational recordings and added grand rounds, but this does not establish comprehensive surgical critical-care, infection/source-control, trauma/burn, endoscopy, MIS, or technical competence. Grand rounds are topic-specific, not systematic lessons across the domain.

Surgical oncology/U11 coverage remains incomplete: breast stage-0 and pancreatic-cancer recordings are narrow talks and do not substitute for staging, multidisciplinary decision-making, tumor biology, evidence appraisal, or outcomes instruction across general surgery.

Verified observed free recordings total 22.1875 hours, of which 8.4136 are categorized specialty and 13.7739 foundation. The 13.8125-hour floor gap remains real; original authored scripts and planned clips are not rendered or counted.

For the 50 pre-existing YouTube items, the original ledger reports durations from public playlist metadata but individual playback was not independently verified because of HTTP 429/403 throttling. The seven added Utah Kaltura pages returned HTTP 200 and exposed durations, player and download links; playback and clinical content were not independently quality-reviewed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A stable adult with suspected uncomplicated appendicitis asks whether surgery is the only evidence-supported option. Which answer is most accurate?

options.text: Selected patients may discuss antibiotic-first management, with recurrence/failure uncertainty; appendectomy remains an accepted option.
Antibiotics are mandatory for all cases and eliminate recurrence.
Appendectomy is prohibited until symptoms persist for 72 hours.
An appendicolith has no effect on selection or counseling.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The WSES 2020 guideline supports discussing non-operative management with antibiotics in selected uncomplicated cases, while counseling on failure/recurrence and selection factors; this is not a blanket substitute for clinical judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with septic shock has imaging showing a perforated viscus. After initial resuscitation and antibiotics, what principle governs source control?

options.text: Defer source control until all laboratory abnormalities normalize.
Rapidly identify the anatomic source and implement required source control as soon as medically and logistically practical.
Continue antimicrobial treatment alone for a fixed 72 hours.
Treat the CT finding as incidental unless cultures are positive.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SSC recommends rapidly identifying/excluding an anatomic source requiring emergent control and implementing it as soon as medically/logistically practical. Prolonged stabilization in lieu of needed source control is generally not advised.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult with adhesive small-bowel obstruction has no peritonitis, strangulation or ischemia. Which initial approach is consistent with WSES guidance?

options.text: A trial of non-operative management with bowel rest, decompression and supportive care, with close reassessment.
Immediate operation is obligatory in every adhesive obstruction.
Discharge without follow-up because most resolve.
Wait indefinitely if nasogastric output remains high.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Bologna guideline supports non-operative management unless peritonitis, strangulation, or ischemia are present; it describes supportive care and cautions that duration requires reassessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fit adult is diagnosed with acute calculous cholecystitis. What broad treatment timing does 2020 WSES recommend when appropriate expertise is available?

options.text: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy as soon as possible, within 7 days of admission and 10 days from symptom onset.
Mandatory interval surgery at 6 months.
Antibiotics indefinitely instead of surgery.
Open operation for every patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The WSES 2020 guideline recommends early laparoscopic cholecystectomy as soon as possible within its specified timing window when expertise is available; individual contraindications/context matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with possible sepsis but no shock has uncertain infection likelihood and a broad differential. Which reasoning is guideline-consistent?

options.text: Reassess infectious and noninfectious explanations promptly; tailor antimicrobial decisions to evolving likelihood and severity.
Assume all postoperative fever is sepsis and use antibiotics indefinitely.
Wait for culture results before any assessment.
Exclude surgical source control from the differential.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SSC emphasizes rapid assessment of likelihood, continued reassessment for alternative diagnoses, and antimicrobial timing according to shock/high-likelihood vs possible sepsis without shock.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hemodynamically stable adult inpatient without a special clinical modifier has hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL. Which statement best reflects AABB 2023 guidance?

options.text: A restrictive transfusion strategy generally considers RBC transfusion below 7 g/dL, interpreted in overall clinical context.
Transfusion is never appropriate below 8 g/dL.
All surgical patients require transfusion below 10 g/dL.
The threshold is a mandatory automatic order irrespective of symptoms/context.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AABB recommends considering transfusion below 7 g/dL for most hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, while urging clinicians to incorporate the overall context and alternatives. This is not an automatic order.

practiceQuestions.stem: During planning for clean-contaminated surgery, a team proposes routine additional prophylactic antibiotics after closure solely because a drain remains. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: CDC-aligned evidence-based guidance advises against additional prophylactic doses after closure for clean/clean-contaminated procedures, even with a drain.
A drain always requires 7 days of prophylaxis.
Topical antibiotic powder is mandatory.
Prophylaxis should be administered only after incision closure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The CDC 2017 SSI guideline published in JAMA Surgery states not to continue additional prophylactic antimicrobial doses after closure in clean and clean-contaminated procedures, even with a drain. Re-check current local protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: A candidate preparing for ABS general surgery certification asks if this course confers eligibility. Which response is correct?

options.text: No. Eligibility depends on ABS requirements, accredited training, operative log/documentation and other criteria; an independent course confers none.
Yes, completion substitutes for residency.
Passing this question bank automatically qualifies the learner for the GSQE.
A Johns Hopkins page alone grants board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABS describes specific accredited residency and other eligibility/documentation requirements; this independent self-study curriculum cannot confer training credit, eligibility or certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: For oral-case reasoning, what response structure most closely aligns with ABS stated GSCE evaluation?

options.text: State a prioritized assessment and logical plan, explain why/how, address critical risks and adapt to new findings.
Recite an operation regardless of stability or diagnostic uncertainty.
Avoid stating uncertainty or limitations.
Focus on obscure diagnoses while omitting common problems.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABS emphasizes organized approach and rationale, interpretation of findings, efficient clinical problem solving, avoiding critical errors, acknowledging limits, and adapting to changing course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public surgical image is visible in an article. What is the appropriate teaching-use rule for this course?

options.text: Link to the source and review its license/terms; visibility alone is not permission to copy or rehost.
Copy every image because the case is de-identified.
Remove the author watermark and reuse it.
Treat all clinical pictures online as public domain.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view does not itself grant reuse rights. The curriculum links authentic educational cases while prohibiting image or patient-record copying and requiring license review.
